s: a cadenza (a part of a piece of music)
a cadence (a progression of at least two chords which conclude a piece of music)
a cadence (a fall in inflection of a speaker’s voice, such as at the end of a sentence)
Kadenz.et: Borrowed from Italian cadenza, from Latin cadentia.

Kadett.et: Borrowed from French cadet. Compare Hunsrik Katett.

s: Womöglich könne jenseits der staatlichen Justiz, unter deren Korruptheit besonders die Ärmsten leiden, die Einsetzung von traditionellen islamischen Richtern (Kadis) befriedend wirken.
Kadi.et: First attested in the 16th century. From Arabic قَاضِي (qāḍī), possibly through a French intermediate French cadi.

s: squad (body of the players of a team or club)
cadre (body of officers forming a new regiment)
cadre (the ideologically trained elite, which is to fill all public and economic leadership positions)
cadre; leader (an individual in the above elite)
a highly skilled or highly motivated person or group of persons

Kaddig.et: Entered German from Low Prussian (German Low German) Kaddig, Kaddik (“juniper”), perhaps as early as the Middle Low German period. From Old Prussian kadegis (“juniper”), from or cognate to Lithuanian kadagys (“juniper”), disputed whether the source or descenda…

s: blind obedience, fanatical or excessive loyalty
Kadavergehorsam.et:
From Kadaver + Gehorsam, lit. "cadaverous obedience", "corpse-obedience" or "corpse-like obedience" (Porter 2013).
Ultimately a rendition of an expression in the Constitutiones by Ignatius of Loyola (1558), qui sub Obedientia vivunt, se ferri ac regi a divina …
